Why Is My Flight Late?

The Hidden Anatomy of U.S. Flight Delays

What 7 million U.S. flight records reveal about when delay risk builds, what sits behind a delay, and what travelers can actually do.

7,043,316scheduled flight records
Jul 2025 – Jun 2026one full year
365 daysdaily operational coverage
40 variablesselected analysis fields
The short version: Earlier departures are generally more reliable — but one delay rate can hide very different operational stories.

Why this story matters. Flight delays are familiar, but the number shown on a departure board is only the end of a longer operational story. For travelers, the useful question is not simply whether delays happen. It is whether delay risk follows a pattern that can support better choices — and whether the same delay percentage can mean very different things behind the scenes.

Who this is for. Travelers who care about schedule reliability, and anyone who uses public airline data to compare operational performance. The goal is to translate a large federal dataset into a small number of patterns that are useful without overstating what the data can prove.

Data source. U.S. DOT Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance. Our analysis covers scheduled records from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026. BTS defines a late arrival as 15 minutes or more after scheduled arrival and publishes separate categories for delayed-flight causes and cancellation causes.

01 · WHEN

Delay risk builds through the day

The first pattern is simple to see and easy to remember: morning is generally more reliable than evening.

At 06:00, the arrival-delay rate is about 9.9%. It rises steadily through the day and reaches about 32.5% around 19:00 before declining to about 19.8% by 23:00. The pattern is not “later is always worse.” It is a build-up toward an evening peak, followed by a late-night decline.

The cause mix changes at the same time. The share of recorded delay minutes attributed to Late Aircraft reaches about 50.1% in the evening. This is consistent with disruption accumulating across an interconnected flight network — but it does not prove that one earlier flight directly caused another flight to be late.

What to remember

The time-of-day pattern is one of the most consistent signals in the project: lower in the morning, highest in the evening, and lower again late at night.

02 · WHY

Why flights delay is not why they cancel

The most surprising contrast appears when delay causes and cancellation causes are placed side by side.

Among recorded delay minutes, Late Aircraft accounts for 39.6%, Carrier-related delay for 33.2%, NAS for 20.8%, Weather for 6.2%, and Security for 0.1%.

Cancellations tell a very different story. Weather accounts for 63.3% of coded cancellations, Carrier for 20.7%, NAS for 15.9%, and Security for 0.1%. To a traveler, both outcomes can feel like “my trip was disrupted.” Operationally, they are not the same problem.

The surprise

Weather dominates cancellations, but it represents only a small share of recorded delay minutes. Late Aircraft is the largest recorded-delay category.

03 · CONTEXT

Same delay rate, same performance?

Not necessarily. A single delay rate is an outcome, not a complete explanation of how that outcome was produced.

“Suppose two airlines both have a 22% delay rate. Would we immediately say they perform at the same level?”

The answer is not necessarily. The same total delay rate can be built from very different operational mixes. The airline fingerprints below compare the shares of recorded delay minutes attributed to Carrier, Weather, NAS, Security, and Late Aircraft.

The composition varies substantially across carriers. For example, Southwest’s recorded delay minutes are heavily concentrated in Late Aircraft (about 51.2%), while United has a much larger NAS share (about 33.3%). Delta’s mix contains a larger Carrier share (about 44.8%) and a smaller Late Aircraft share (about 29.6%) than several other major carriers. These are descriptive profiles, not quality scores.

Why this matters

One percentage can compress very different operational stories into the same number. Raw airline or airport rankings therefore need context — including route mix, schedule, geography, and network structure.

04 · ACTION

If avoiding delays matters, fly earlier

Once the system looks complicated, the practical question becomes: what can a traveler actually control?

Hold everything else constant for a moment. If you care a lot about avoiding a delay because you have a connection, meeting, or fixed schedule, departure time is one of the clearest choices available to you.

The heatmap shows two things at once. Day of week still shifts the risk, but the time-of-day pattern is more consistent. On Thursday, the arrival-delay rate is about 7.5% in the 00–05 block and about 34.7% in the 18–20 block. At 18–20, Tuesday is about 26.3% while Sunday is about 38.9%. Weekday matters, but the broad morning-to-evening pattern remains visible.

Practical takeaway

If reducing delay risk is a priority and you have flexibility, an earlier departure is generally the safer choice in this dataset. It is a probability pattern, not a guarantee for an individual flight.

05 · ROBUSTNESS

Does the pattern survive a broader definition?

A useful finding should survive reasonable changes in measurement. So we challenged our own delay metric.

Our primary arrival-delay measure uses ARR_DEL15 and therefore focuses on flights with a valid arrival outcome. Cancelled flights are not treated as on time; they are outside that arrival-delay denominator. From a traveler’s perspective, however, a cancellation or diversion is also a disruption.

We therefore classified all 7,043,316 scheduled records into completed/not delayed at least 15 minutes, completed/delayed at least 15 minutes, cancelled, diverted, or unknown/inconsistent. There was one unknown/inconsistent record. For a broader reliability view, we then combined delayed, cancelled, and diverted flights. This is not a severity score: a cancellation is not equivalent to a 15-minute delay.

By 23:00, combined disruption falls to about 21.2%. The same broad shape remains: morning lower, evening peak, late-night decline. The evening peak is therefore not simply an artifact of excluding cancellations or diversions from the original arrival-delay denominator.

Why this strengthens the story

We found the time-of-day pattern, questioned whether the denominator could create it, changed the measurement, and observed the same broad shape again.

06 · LIMITS & ETHICS

What the data can — and cannot — tell us

The strongest public data stories are explicit about denominators, uncertainty, and the limits of interpretation.

Descriptive, not causal. These analyses identify associations in observed operations. They do not establish that departure time, an airport, an airline, or a prior flight caused a specific delay.
Raw rankings are unadjusted. Airline and airport rates reflect different route mixes, schedules, geography, network structures, and exposure to weather or congestion. They should not be read as pure quality scores.
Flights are not passengers. Each scheduled flight is one record. The analysis is not weighted by passenger counts, so it describes flight-level reliability rather than the number of people affected.
Cause fields have reporting rules. BTS requires cause information for late and cancelled flights under federal reporting definitions. These fields are useful operational labels, but they are not a complete structural causal model of the aviation system.
Different disruptions have different impacts. The broader outcome measure combines delayed, cancelled, and diverted flights only to test reliability patterns. It should not be interpreted as saying those experiences are equally severe.
Ethical use of public operational data. The dataset contains flight operations rather than personal traveler records. The larger ethical risk is interpretation: an unadjusted ranking can unfairly stigmatize an airline or airport if readers mistake correlation for operational quality or causation.
TAKEAWAY

What should you remember?

01

Earlier flights are generally more reliable

The morning-to-evening pattern appears in the original delay rate, the heatmap, and the broader disruption measure.

02

One delay rate does not tell the whole story

The same outcome can reflect very different mixes of Carrier, NAS, Weather, Security, and Late Aircraft delay.

03

Delay and cancellation are different problems

Late Aircraft dominates recorded delay minutes; Weather dominates coded cancellations.

A flight delay is rarely just about one flight.

If you have flexibility and reliability matters, the clearest practical signal in this dataset is simple: flying earlier is generally the safer bet.

  • BTS table profile and dataset description
  • BTS Technical Directive No. 39 — On-Time Reporting 2025
  • BTS Technical Directive No. 40 — On-Time Reporting 2026
  • GitHub repository — code, README, and reproducibility workflow
  • Project data release — merged July 2025 to June 2026 dataset
All percentages and figures in this story are produced from the project’s final analysis outputs. Delay-cause shares refer to recorded BTS delay minutes; cancellation shares refer to coded cancelled flights. Dates use scheduled local departure blocks where shown.

Reproducibility in four steps

  1. Obtain the merged project release or the monthly BTS source files for July 2025 through June 2026.
  2. Follow the repository README to reconstruct the merged dataset and verify the expected schema and date coverage.
  3. Run the numbered scripts in the analysis/ folder in sequence, beginning with the data-quality audit.
  4. Compare the generated chart_data/ summaries and charts/ figures with the published outputs in this story.

Key measures

MeasureMeaning
ARR_DEL151 when a completed flight arrives at least 15 minutes late; the primary arrival-delay indicator.
CANCELLEDBTS cancellation flag; cancelled flights are outside the ARR_DEL15 arrival-delay denominator.
DIVERTEDBTS diversion flag; included in the broader all-scheduled-record reliability check.
Delay minutesRecorded minutes by Carrier, Weather, NAS, Security, and Late Aircraft cause categories.
Cancellation codeBTS-coded cancellation category: Carrier, Weather, NAS, or Security.
